title.official: When third party claim may be filed

variants.BOOK_A: WhenThird Party Claim May be Filed

division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.44   A defendant or third party defendant may file a third party
claim against another person who
(a) is or might be liable to the party filing the third party
claim for all or part of the claim against that party,
(b) is or might be liable to the party filing the third party
claim for an independent claim arising out of
(i) a transaction or occurrence or series of transactions
or occurrences involved in the action between the
plaintiff and the defendant, or
(ii) a related transaction or occurrence or series of related
transactions or occurrences,
or
(c) should be bound by a decision about an issue between the
plaintiff and the defendant.

BOOK_B.title: When third party claim may be filed

commentary.text: Rule 3.44 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.44. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R. 72, 79 Alta. L.R. (5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes discussed claims for contribution. At paragraphs 201–205, her Ladyship said: 201 A right to recover contribution arises under statute, specifically under s 3 of the Tort-feasors Act and the Contributory Negligence Act, RSA 2000, c C-27 [the Contributory Negligence Act], and under the common law: MacKay v. Farm Business Consultants Inc, 2006 ABCA 316 at paras 9–12 [MacKay]. 202 The types of third party claims that can be filed under the new Rules include the classic type of third party claims for contribution described under Rule 3.44(a). They now also include third party claims against a party who is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for an independent claim (Rule 3.44(b)), or who should be bound by a decision about an issue between the plaintiff and the defendant (Rule 3.44(c)). 1. — Claims for contribution under the common law 203 The Defendants have a right to recover contribution from the Third Parties under the common law, if the Third Parties breached duties they owed directly to the Defendants under contract, tort, statute or otherwise. The right to contribution arises if the damage the Defendants allege they suffered as a result of the Third Parties' breaches are related to the damage that the Plaintiff, CNRL, alleges it suffered as a result of the Defendants' breaches. Because the common law right to contribution arises if the Third Parties breached duties owed directly to the Defendants, it exists independently of any claim that CNRL may have against the Third Parties and can support an independent cause of action against the Third Parties. 204 The nature of the common law claim for contribution, and the distinction between a third party claim for contribution under the common law and under the Tort-feasors Act, was described by Conrad JA in Leoppky at paras 30–33: […] Generally, a defendant may third party a person to enforce a duty or obligation owed by the third party to the defendant which relates to the same damages pled in the statement of claim. For example, where a customer purchases defective goods and sues the vendor, that vendor may be able to third party the manufacturer who supplied the defective goods. That is because the vendor can allege a separate duty owed to it by the manufacturer which could support an independent cause of action giving rise to third party liability. The [defendants] have not alleged any such independent duty or obligation in their third party notice. The facts pled do not disclose any contract, duty of care or statutory obligation owed by [the third party] to the [defendants] which would entitle them to any claim against or contribution from [the third party]. Thus, the third party notice discloses no possible third party liability on [the third party's] part. As noted by this Court in Metz v. Breland (1990), 76 Alta. L.R (2d) 397 (C.A.), a third party notice serves to enforce duties owed by the third party to the defendant, not to enforce duties owed by the third party to the plaintiff. That is the key test which the [defendants] have not met—to demonstrate that there is some duty owed by [the third party] to them […] 205 In the recent decision of Master Schlosser in Pagnucco v. Sears Canada Inc, 2011 ABQB 810 [Pagnucco], a third party claim for contribution was brought under both the Tort-feasors Act and the common law. The Master described the claim for contribution under the common law at para 17: The proposed Third Party Notice has two distinct parts. One part is based on the duties and obligations the proposed Third Party allegedly owed the Defendant. These allegations are pleaded in breach of contract, breach of warranty, negligence and misrepresentation. There is no doubt that these allegations could form the basis of a free standing claim, although the measure of damages might, to a certain extent, relate to the injuries suffered by the Plaintiff. [emphasis added] At paragraphs 241-242; 245 Hughes, J. said: 241 The validity of the third party claims in the Two Actions also depends in part on the types of third party claims that can be made under the Rules. As the Rules have evolved, they have broadened the circumstances under which a party may file a third party claim: see discussion in Dean v. Kociniak, 2001 ABQB 412, 289 AR 201 [Dean]; and the ALRI 2004 Report on Joining Claims and Parties at paras 139–163. 242 The new Rules allow third party claims to enforce claims for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act or the common law, both of which depend upon the success of the plaintiff's claim against the defendant: Rule 3.44(a). The new Rules also allow a third party claim to be filed against a party who is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for an independent claim, if the independent claims are related to the matters in the main action (Rule 3.44(b)), and against a party who should be bound by a decision about an issue between the plaintiff and the defendant (Rule 3.44 (c)). … 245 Rule 3.44(a) gives broader rights than former Rule 66(1). Rule 66(1) allowed a defendant to make a third party claim where the defendant claimed against any person “that the person is or may be liable to him for all or part of the plaintiff's claim against him.”[emphasis added]. Rule 3.44(a) now provides that a party may file a third party claim against a person who “is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for all or part of the claim against that party”[emphasis added]. As a result, third party claims under Rule 3.44(a) now include both third party claims for contribution arising under the Tort-feasors Act or the common law, the types of third party claims described in paragraphs (1) and (2) of para 123 of the ALRI 2004 Report on Joining Claims and Parties. Justice Hughes provided the following summary regarding third party claims under the common law (at paragraphs 249–251): 249 A claim for contribution under the common law arises when a third party breaches a duty in contract, a common law duty of care or a statutory obligation owed by the third party to the defendant: Leoppky at para 30. 250 Because it is a claim for contribution, it stands or falls based on the outcome of the plaintiff's claim against the defendant. This does not mean that it is derived from the plaintiff's claim against the third party. It does not depend upon the plaintiff having a claim against the third party. A common law claim for contribution is a free-standing claim: Supreme Steel. It arises out of the breach of a separate duty owed by the third party to the defendant “which could support an independent cause of action”: Loeppky at para 30. 251 A third party claim through which a common law claim for contribution is asserted is described as a claim alleging that the “duty or obligation owed by the third party to the defendant … relates to the same damages pled in the statement of claim”[emphasis added]: Leoppky at para 30. A third party claim for contribution under the common law must therefore allege facts that could support a finding that the third party's breach of duty to the defendant caused the defendant to suffer damage that is related to the damage that the plaintiff claims it suffered as a result of the defendant's breach of duty to the plaintiff. And with respect to third party claims for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act, she said at paragraphs 252–258: 252 As is the case with a claim for contribution under the common law, a claim for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act stands or falls based on the outcome of the plaintiff's claim against the defendant. If the claim is a third party claim for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act, the third party claim must allege facts that could support a finding that the third party's breach of duty caused the plaintiff to suffer the same damage that the plaintiff claims it suffered as a result of the defendant's breach of duty to the plaintiff. As discussed, a claimant for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act must also establish that the third party would if sued be liable for the damage suffered by the plaintiff. 253 It is clear that a claim for contribution arises under the Tort-feasors Act when a third party breaches a duty of care in tort owed by the third party to the plaintiff. A defendant asserting a claim for contribution under the Tort-feasors Act on this basis asserts the claim that the plaintiff could have asserted but did not. It is a derivative claim. 254 The Defendants argue that a claim for contribution arises under the Tort-feasors Act can also arise when a third party breaches a duty, in either contract or tort, owed by the third party to the defendant, if that breach of duty causes the defendant to breach a duty to the plaintiff, which causes the plaintiff to suffer the same damage that it alleges was caused by the defendant. The following cases suggest that a claim may arise in these circumstances: Deboer at para 5; Wallace at paras 39, 55, and 56; MacKay at para 12; Howalta, per O'Ferrall JA at paras 77 and 85. —Independent Third Party Claims 255 An independent third party claim arises when the third party breaches a duty owed to the defendant, which causes the defendant to suffer losses that are factually related to the losses suffered by the plaintiff. A true third party claim for contribution is dependent upon the outcome of the plaintiff's action against the defendant. An independent claim for contribution arises from unrelated matters and is not dependent on the outcome of the plaintiff's action against the defendant: Supreme Steel at para 9. —Claims for contribution under the Rules 256 Under the new Rules, a third party claim may be filed against a party who is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for all or part of the claim against that party: Rule 3.44(a). This type of third party claim is asserted to recover a claim for contribution under the common law or the Tort-feasors Act: ALRI 2004 Report on Joining Claims and Parties at para 123. 257 Rule 3.44(b) now also allows third party claims to be filed against a party who is or might be liable to the party filing the third party claim for an independent claim if it is sufficiently related as that is defined in that Rule. 258 Rule 3.44(c) also allows a third party claim to be filed against a party who should be bound by a decision about an issue between the plaintiff and the defendant.
